titulo.texto: Wixárika Ceremonial Outfit (Embroidery, Beads, and Deer)

frase_gancho.texto: Embroidered clothing where every deer and every flower is a prayer.

puente_narrativo.texto: This embroidered clothing has modern relatives. Look along the edges of the hall for a stained-glass window of intense colors and some string screens, made by twentieth-century artists inspired by this mountain range.

guion_corto.texto: This Wixárika (Huichol) man’s outfit consists of a shirt and trousers of white cotton cloth, embroidered with red, blue, and yellow threads in cross-stitch. Along the edges of the sleeves, the collar, and the trousers appear peyote flowers, deer, and other sacred beings. Woven bags embroidered with the same symbols hang from the waist, and a palm-leaf hat decorated with feathers and tassels sits on the head. This clothing is worn in ceremonies and on the pilgrimage. Whoever wears it is dressed in the prayers and stories of their people, and every stitch is a way of asking for protection.

guion_largo.texto:
Notice that what you saw in the Nierika is repeated here. The deer, the peyote flowers, the sun: they are embroidered on the clothing, not glued to a board. A Wixárika who dresses for a ceremony puts on the very same story that is painted in a picture. In their culture, clothing and the body are also places where the sacred world becomes visible.

The basic technique is cross-stitch: two diagonal stitches that form an X, repeated until they make the design. It is a technique thought to have arrived with the Spanish, but the Wixárika people made it their own until it became unmistakable. They use red, blue, yellow, and green threads, and the white cloth works like a sheet of paper on which they draw with a needle. Doing it well takes many hours, and it is usually the work of the whole family: some spin, others embroider, and others sew.

Look at the hat. It has bird feathers and wool tassels, and sometimes beads. The feathers are an adornment, but also an offering, because the bird that flies connects the earth with the sky. Do you remember the feathers of the headdress in the Mexica Hall and the macaws that were raised in Paquimé? Feathers have been a treasure throughout this history, and here they still are.

The bags hanging from the waist are used to keep everyday items and also to carry ceremonial objects. They are woven on a backstrap loom, like the sashes, and decorated with the same motifs. That way of weaving is the one you saw a moment ago in the [textile collection](mna_s12_acervo_textil); here you see it applied to a garment with a specific purpose.

The Wixárika people are also famous for chaquira, those tiny glass beads. Before beads arrived from Europe, seeds, shells, and stones were used. Today gourds, masks, and animal figures are covered with beads, attached with wax, in an art that has gone around the world. It is another way of turning patience into beauty.

Those who make these sacred journeys usually hold posts for several years. The jicareros, for example, serve for five years as representatives of the ancestors and look after the temples and the sacred objects. They wear this clothing as part of an obligation to their community. It is not a party outfit, but an outfit of service.

Something important: this is not costume clothing. In many communities in the mountains it is still worn every day, and at festivals and pilgrimages it is worn with greater care. The museum’s outfit shows the dress version. If one day you see a Wixárika walking through a city in traditional clothing, you will know that they are not wearing a costume, but a way of being.

This hall reminds us that beauty is not always in a display case. Sometimes it walks through the streets, in the clothing of the one who wears it, and becomes prayer with every step.

texto.Technique/Material: Embroidered cotton cloth, backstrap loom, glass beads, feathers, and palm
texto.Function: Ceremonial dress of sacred authorities and initiates (gourd bearers)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Huichol dress in so many colors just to attract the attention of visitors.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Every embroidered design has meaning: deer, peyote flowers, and other sacred beings protect the wearer, especially in ceremonies and pilgrimages.
